claims.text: A 36-year-old man with acromegaly diagnosed in 2018 from a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, whose acromegaly symptoms persisted despite trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy in 2018, presented to the emergency department with acute shortness of breath, high-grade fever, chest pain and cough of a day's duration; the cough produced whitish sputum without hemoptysis. He had no recent travel, surgery or prolonged immobility and no past or family history of thrombotic events.

claims.text: On examination he was normotensive, febrile, tachypneic and tachycardic, with oxygen saturation of 87% on room air requiring supplemental oxygen, and had typical acromegaly features. Chest X-ray showed increased bronchovascular markings but was otherwise normal, the ECG showed sinus tachycardia and incomplete right bundle branch block, and echocardiography showed moderately increased right ventricular systolic pressure suggesting right ventricular strain. Initial blood tests showed mild leukocytosis, slightly elevated CRP and a negative D-dimer, and the Wells score gave a low probability.

claims.text: Because of high clinical suspicion despite the negative D-dimer, an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed a bilateral massive pulmonary embolism. He was promptly started on therapeutic subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin and transferred to the high-dependency unit, then, after endocrinology and pulmonology consultation, transitioned to rivaroxaban while treatment for his diabetes and hypertension continued. After treatment he improved and was discharged in a stable condition on rivaroxaban, with outpatient follow-up planned at the clinic.
